prompt: A new Precision Nutrition Level 1 client wants a complete diet by Friday. What is your first coaching move?

options.text: Help them notice current eating and pick one small next action
Hand over a 12-week contest menu with macros for every meal
Start a 30-day elimination diet to find hidden food triggers
Set a weekly pound-loss quota so they feel urgency from day one

explanation: PN Level 1 is client-centered: first build awareness of what they already do, then one small, owned action. Dumping a contest meal plan, an elimination protocol, or an imposed scale quota is expert-centered prescription, closer to meal-plan sales or medical nutrition therapy than coaching.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coaching with a day-one meal-plan dump; a full contest menu overloads a new client and skips awareness.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a clinical elimination protocol with a first coaching step; that work belongs with an RDN, not week-one habits.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an imposed outcome target with a first action; PN starts with behaviors the client can control.

prompt: A client texts after a wedding weekend: “I blew it. I’m a failure.” What should you do first?

options.text: Restart the whole program from week one as a clean reset
Get curious about what happened and what still went well
Add extra cardio this week to offset the weekend calories
Tighten their weekend calorie cap so it cannot happen again

explanation: Treat the weekend as data, not drama. Curiosity shows what got in the way, what they still did, and what to adjust. Shame, program restarts, compensatory training, or tighter restriction after a lapse all feed all-or-nothing thinking instead of outcome-based coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses one hard weekend with total program failure; restarting from scratch discards useful data and progress.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses nutrition coaching with CPT ‘earn it back’ programming; extra cardio frames food as a debt to punish.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a lapse with a reason to restrict harder; tighter caps after a blowout often drive the next one.

prompt: You have a week of check-in data: walks were skipped, sleep was poor, and the scale is noisy. Outcome-based decision making says you:

options.text: Keep the original plan frozen until the 12-week reassessment
Choose the next step only from their original intake goals
Adjust the next action from what they did and how they feel
Change the plan after two down days on the bathroom scale

explanation: Outcome-based decisions use recent behaviors, recovery, and how the client feels—not the plan on paper. You change the next small action from that evidence. Waiting 12 weeks, clinging to intake wishes, or reacting to two noisy scale days all ignore the data you already have.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a long program calendar with outcome-based coaching; freezing the plan for 12 weeks ignores live data.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses intake wishes with current evidence; starting goals set direction, not the next weekly action.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses two-day scale noise with a meaningful outcome; PN weighs habits, sleep, and performance over time.

prompt: Which first habit best fits a Precision Nutrition Level 1 start?

options.text: A full meal plan they must follow at breakfast, lunch, and dinner
Three new habits at once so they feel early momentum this week
Daily calorie tracking in an app before any other coaching work
One clear, small, repeatable behavior they can do on a weekday

explanation: Simple and sequential: one clear behavior they can repeat on an ordinary day (protein at breakfast, a 10-minute walk). A full meal plan, a three-habit stack, or mandatory calorie logging are multi-skill loads that crush early adherence.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a first habit with a whole-diet prescription; a meal plan is many behaviors at once, not one practice.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses momentum with stacking; several new habits at once lowers follow-through under 5S sequential coaching.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a high-effort tracking skill with a first habit; logging every calorie is rarely week-one work.

prompt: Two useful habits compete and the client is already overloaded. You:

options.text: Pick the one they can still do on a genuinely bad day
Pick the one with the biggest predicted fat-loss impact
Pick the one you personally think matters most as coach
Run both habits this week and see which one sticks first

explanation: Early 5S coaching prefers simple and supported: the habit that survives a bad day beats the theoretically ‘best’ habit. Coach preference and dual-habit experiments add friction. Adherence on a hard day is the filter.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses theoretical fat-loss impact with doability; the highest-yield habit fails if it dies under stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses expert-centered ranking with client-centered sizing; your priority is not their confidence.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a test with focus; running competing habits dilutes effort instead of choosing the sustainable one.

prompt: A client will not log food in an app. How can you still coach nutrition behaviors?

options.text: Give a rigid meal plan so they never have to choose foods
Use plate photos, hand portions, or a one-item checklist
Rely on weekly weigh-ins as the only progress measure you review
Wait to start coaching until they agree to daily logging

explanation: Meet them where they are. Plate methods, photos, hand portions, and single-item checklists still create awareness without requiring a food log. A rigid menu, scale-only reviews, or refusing to coach until they log all raise the barrier instead of lowering it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses refusal to log with a reason for a stricter menu; a full plan is usually a bigger demand than tracking.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses body weight with behavior data; the scale misses the habits photos or checklists can still capture.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one tracking method with readiness to be coached; logging is optional, not an entry ticket.

prompt: Every new habit meets pushback in session. In PN coaching that resistance usually means:

options.text: Motivation is low, so raise the stakes with public deadlines
The plan is too easy, so you should add more challenge right away
Ambivalence is present; explore it with questions, not a lecture
They are noncompliant, so restate the program rules more clearly

explanation: Resistance is usually mixed feelings, not laziness. Better questions surface change talk; lectures, public pressure, extra challenge, and rule recitals all escalate pushback. Client-centered coaching treats ambivalence as information.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses ambivalence with a motivation deficit you can scare away; deadlines often raise resistance.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses pushback with boredom; resistance more often means the ask is too big or not wanted.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses coaching with compliance policing; restating rules is a lecture, not motivational interviewing.

prompt: How should a PN coach handle a request for body progress photos?

options.text: Make photos mandatory at intake before coaching can begin at all
Treat signup as consent to share before-and-after shots
Take the photos yourself in the gym after each session
Keep them optional, private, and used only with consent

explanation: Body photos are optional, stored privately, and used only with specific consent. Payment, intake, or a coach-held camera does not authorize capture or posting. Client-centered coaching protects body autonomy and never makes photos a condition of help.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a useful metric with a coaching condition; mandatory photos ignore consent and body-image risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses paying for coaching with permission to publish images; sharing needs separate, explicit consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coach control with client control; gym-hallway photos after every session remove their choice.

prompt: A client has missed three weekly check-ins in a row. Your best next step is to:

options.text: Reach out with a short, kind note that makes rejoining easy
Pause their account until they email an apology for missing
Send a reminder of the commitment they signed at onboarding
Assign extra habits so they catch up on all missed weeks

explanation: Re-engagement is the skill: a short, kind, low-friction invite back. Ghosting, guilt about the contract, or extra homework after a lapse all raise the cost of returning. Shrink the next ask so they can re-enter this week.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a pause with coaching; freezing the account without a warm reach-out is effectively ghosting.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a signed form with re-engagement; pointing to the contract adds guilt instead of a path back.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses missed weeks with a reason to add load; extra habits punish the client who is already struggling.

prompt: Weight is unchanged, but the client slept better and cooked three dinners. Why mention those wins?

options.text: The scale remains the only outcome that truly counts here
Behaviors and energy often shift before the scale moves
Non-scale wins distract from fat loss and should be ignored
Wins should stay hidden until the fat-loss goal is fully met

explanation: Non-scale victories keep the feedback loop alive. Sleep, cooking, energy, and skill often move before weight. Celebrating those behaviors is outcome-based, not a distraction. Scale-only coaching trains clients to quit when the number is noisy.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses one biomarker with the whole outcome set; PN tracks behaviors, energy, and skills, not only weight.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses process wins with a side show; ignoring them removes the data that usually precedes fat loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses delayed praise with discipline; hiding wins until a goal weight kills the reinforcement loop.

prompt: After a ‘perfect’ eating week the client rebounds. What is more useful than chasing perfect weeks?

options.text: Strict weekdays followed by an unrestricted weekend reward
Two perfect days each week with no plan for the other five
An 80–90 percent week they can repeat without a rebound
A fresh Monday restart each time they slip on the weekend

explanation: Consistency beats heroics. An 80–90% week they can repeat outperforms a perfect week that collapses. Strict-then-free cycles, isolated perfect days, and weekly Monday resets are all-or-nothing patterns, not sustainable coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a reward weekend with sustainability; strict-then-free cycles mimic restrict-binge eating.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses two hero days with a weekly pattern; isolated perfect days are not a repeatable practice.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a Monday reset with consistency; weekly restarts encode all-or-nothing thinking.

prompt: You ask, “On a scale of 1–10, how confident are you that you can do this habit?” You are mainly checking:

options.text: Whether they can recite the biochemistry behind the habit
Whether guilt is high enough to force compliance this week
Whether they should add training volume if the habit feels easy
Whether the habit is sized so they expect to follow through

explanation: A confidence rating is a sizing tool. Low numbers mean shrink or simplify the habit until they can say 8–9/10. It is not a quiz, a guilt check, or a cue to add CPT training volume. Follow-through tracks expected confidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses confidence with knowledge testing; knowing the science does not mean the habit is doable this week.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses confidence with shame-based compliance; guilt is a poor predictor of repeatable action.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a nutrition-habit check with CPT programming; ease of a food habit is not a reason to add volume.

prompt: You realize you talked for most of a 20-minute check-in. That usually means:

You built rapport faster by filling silence with your advice

prompt: A client wants to overhaul protein, sleep, steps, and alcohol this week. Using PN’s 5S approach, you:

options.text: Launch all four changes together so they feel a complete reset
Write a periodized lifting mesocycle because this is CPT programming

prompt: A client is in a moderate calorie deficit and still lifting three days a week. What is protein’s most useful coaching job here?

options.text: Serve as the main fuel for those high-intensity lifting sessions
Raise metabolism enough that the deficit is no longer needed
Supply essential fatty acids the body uses to make hormones
Support fullness and muscle retention while calories stay lower

explanation: In a deficit, protein’s practical job is satiety plus helping retain lean mass when training continues. It is not the primary high-intensity fuel, and its extra thermic cost is too small to replace an energy gap. Essential fatty acids come from dietary fat, not protein.

distractorExplanations.a: Carbohydrate (muscle glycogen) is the main fuel for hard lifting; protein’s coaching role is fullness and muscle retention.
distractorExplanations.b: Protein’s higher thermic effect is real but small; it cannot cancel a calorie deficit or replace fat-loss math.
distractorExplanations.c: Essential fatty acids come from fat; protein does not supply them and is not a hormone-fat substitute.

prompt: A client lost about 8 lb across 10 weeks on a mixed-macro plan. What best explains the fat-loss portion of that change?

options.text: A sustained calorie deficit across those weeks
Mostly the first-week glycogen and water drop
Fat loss that only happens when carbs stay very low
Day-to-day scale noise from sodium and gut contents

explanation: Meaningful fat loss still requires a sustained energy deficit, whatever the carb level. First-week drops and daily swings are mostly water, glycogen, sodium, and gut contents. Low-carb can help some people eat less, but it is not the only path to a deficit.

distractorExplanations.b: Early scale drops are mostly glycogen and water; they do not explain weeks of fat loss on a mixed-macro plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Fat loss follows energy balance on high- or low-carb patterns; low-carb is one way to create a deficit, not a requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily weight noise is water, sodium, and gut contents; it is not the fat-loss trend across 10 weeks.

prompt: A client wants to strip almost all dietary fat “to get lean faster.” What should you teach about fat at Precision Nutrition Level 1?

options.text: It is mainly needed to absorb water-soluble vitamins such as C and B12
It supports hormones, fat-soluble vitamins, and meal satisfaction
It is the main structural building block used to grow new muscle
It is the primary fuel for short, high-intensity sprint efforts

explanation: Dietary fat is not optional window dressing. Clients need some fat for hormones, absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K, and meals they can stick with. Extreme fat cuts often backfire as hunger and adherence problems, and they do not magically outrun energy balance.

distractorExplanations.a: Fat helps absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), not water-soluble vitamin C and B vitamins.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein, not fat, is the main structural macronutrient for muscle tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Short, hard efforts run mainly on carbohydrate; fat is a larger fuel at lower intensities.

prompt: A recreational lifter asks if they should drop carbs to near zero to get lean. What is the best coach-level answer?

options.text: Carbs are nonessential, so cutting them is the fastest fat-loss path
Carbs drive fat gain mainly through insulin, even in a deficit
Carbs are useful training fuel and can still fit a fat-loss plan
Carbs should be eaten mostly at breakfast and avoided after 6 p.m.

explanation: Precision Nutrition Level 1 does not treat carbohydrate as a toxin. Carbs fuel higher-intensity training and can sit inside a calorie deficit. Fat loss is not reserved for keto, insulin is not the main fat-gain switch, and clock-based carb bans rarely beat total intake and training needs.

distractorExplanations.a: A deficit—not a carb ban—drives fat loss; many clients lose fat while still eating carbs around training.
distractorExplanations.b: The carbohydrate-insulin story is not the main cause of fat gain; sustained energy surplus is.
distractorExplanations.d: Time-of-day carb rules matter far less than total intake and putting carbs where training needs them.

prompt: A client feels hungry between meals and constipated on a low-produce diet. What is fiber’s main coaching benefit?

options.text: Driving muscle protein synthesis after lifting sessions
Improving uptake of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K
Speeding glycogen refill in the hours after hard training
Supporting fullness and more regular digestion day to day

explanation: Fiber from plants is a satiety and GI-regularity tool. It is not a substitute for protein after lifting, not a fat-soluble vitamin carrier, and not a fast glycogen refill. For a hungry, constipated client, more produce and other fiber sources is the practical first move.

distractorExplanations.a: Muscle protein synthesis depends on protein and training stimulus, not on fiber grams.
distractorExplanations.b: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption needs dietary fat; fiber is not the uptake vehicle.
distractorExplanations.c: Rapid glycogen refill uses faster-digesting carbohydrate; fiber slows, not speeds, that process.

prompt: A client “forgets” weekend drinks in the food log and fat loss has stalled. What should you teach about alcohol?

options.text: Count it as carbohydrate grams, the same as table sugar

prompt: A client wants one hydration rule they can follow on busy workdays. What is the safest basic advice?

Wait until thirst is intense before taking any fluids at all

prompt: A client wants to “cover nutrition” with a large pill stack instead of changing meals. What is the best first-line micronutrient advice?

prompt: A client is upset about a 4 lb jump on the scale the morning after a salty restaurant dinner. What usually explains that change?

options.text: Glycogen, sodium, and gut contents shifting overnight
About four pounds of new body fat from that one meal
Several pounds of muscle broken down while they slept
Immediate metabolic collapse from one higher-calorie day

explanation: Overnight swings of a few pounds are almost always water, glycogen, sodium, and gut contents. Four pounds of fat would require on the order of 14,000 extra kcal. Muscle does not vanish overnight, and metabolic adaptation is slow and small—not a one-night 4 lb event.

distractorExplanations.b: Four pounds of fat would need roughly 14,000 extra kcal; one restaurant meal cannot do that.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscle cannot be lost in that amount overnight; rapid jumps are fluid and GI contents.
distractorExplanations.d: Adaptive thermogenesis is gradual; it does not drop body weight 4 lb by the next morning.

prompt: A client treats a 1,200-kcal app target as “my metabolism” and wants to eat that forever. How should you explain resting metabolic rate?

options.text: It is the same number as total daily energy expenditure
It is energy used at rest to keep the body running
It is only the calories burned during planned workouts
It is only the energy spent digesting and absorbing meals

explanation: RMR is resting energy cost—keeping organs and tissues going—not the whole day’s burn. TDEE also includes daily movement, exercise, and the thermic effect of food. App outputs are estimates, not a medical prescription to live at 1,200 kcal.

distractorExplanations.a: TDEE is rest plus movement, exercise, and food processing; RMR is only the resting piece.
distractorExplanations.c: Workout calories are exercise activity, one slice of TDEE, not resting metabolic rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Energy used to digest food is TEF, a small TDEE slice, not RMR.

prompt: A client wants to “hack metabolism” by eating only protein shakes. What is true of the thermic effect of food at coach level?

options.text: A small slice of daily burn, and highest for dietary fat
The largest slice of daily burn, bigger than resting metabolism
A small slice of daily burn, and highest for protein
A large slice of daily burn, and highest for carbohydrate

explanation: TEF is real and modest—often around 10% of TDEE—and protein costs more to process than carb or fat. That does not make an all-shake diet a metabolism cheat code. Resting metabolism is still the biggest daily burn, and fat has the lowest thermic effect.

distractorExplanations.a: Fat has the lowest thermic effect (roughly 0–3%); protein, not fat, is the highest.
distractorExplanations.b: RMR is the largest TDEE component; TEF is a small slice, not larger than rest.
distractorExplanations.d: TEF is not a large share of TDEE, and carbohydrate is not the highest-thermic macro.

prompt: A client on about 1,000 kcal is exhausted, cold, and sleeping poorly. What is the best next coaching move?

Push caffeine so they can keep training through the fatigue

distractorExplanations.b: Caffeine can mask tiredness without fixing low energy availability; it is not the coaching fix.

prompt: A client asks whether creatine monohydrate is “worth taking.” What is the Precision Nutrition Level 1-appropriate answer?

distractorExplanations.d: Creatine’s best-supported uses are short, high-intensity and strength efforts, not endurance-only.
